title: Bishop and knight III: the whole mate
summary: Deliver the whole bishop and knight mate with Delétang's triangles, without falling into the traps along the way.
part.bigNet.title: The big triangle
part.bigNet.summary: The bishop closes the b1–h7 diagonal and the white king walks round behind the black king.
part.midNet.title: The middle triangle
part.midNet.summary: The triangle shrinks: the bishop jumps to the smaller diagonal and the knight hurries to close the dark squares.
part.smallNet.title: The small triangle
part.smallNet.summary: The bishop's last jump and the mating pattern in the h1 corner.
part.seal.title: The dark squares
part.seal.summary: The bishop's diagonal alone doesn't trap the black king. The exits on the dark squares are the knight's job.
part.route.title: The right diagonal
part.route.summary: Before the bishop enters a diagonal, see which light squares it gives up.
part.loose.title: Loose pieces
part.loose.summary: When an attacked piece is far from your king, look for a check that defends it at the same time.
part.rhine.title: The stalemating check
part.rhine.summary: Near the corner, count the black king's squares before giving check, or you fall into Rhine's trap.
part.kempinski.title: Kempinski–Epishin
part.kempinski.summary: In a game between grandmasters, the defending king hides in the wrong corner. Then the whole mate in the practical challenge.
step.t_big: This is the position Bruce Pandolfini uses in his book Endgame Workshop to teach Delétang's method. The black king, on d2, can no longer cross the b1–h7 diagonal. Your king, on b2, is on the outside. How do you bring the white king over to the black king's side without opening an exit?
step.t_big.hint1: Before moving the king, see which squares it watches now, on b2, and which square the black king fights it for.
step.t_big.hint2: The bishop can move along its own diagonal and watch a square on the first rank.
step.big: In lesson II you drove the black king to the edge; in lesson I, the W got it out of the wrong corner. Today, the triangle method takes it all the way to the right corner. 1.Bc2 is the start of Pandolfini's line. The bishop watches the whole b1–h7 diagonal from any square on it; the knight on e6 takes d4, c5, f4 and g5, the dark squares next to the diagonal; the king on b2 takes c1 and c3. The black king lives in a triangle running from c1 to h1 and up to h6: Delétang's big triangle. From c2 the bishop also takes d1 away from the black king, and the white king can walk round behind it along the first rank. If the black king runs to a8, the other light corner, the three triangles' diagonals are a2–g8, a4–e8 and a6–c8.
step.d_big: Watch the white king's walk. The bishop never leaves the b1–h7 diagonal.
step.d_big.m1: 1.Bc2. The bishop stays on the diagonal and now also takes d1. The black king is left with only e1, e2 and e3.
step.d_big.m2: 1...Ke3. The black king backs off; d4 and f4 belong to the knight, so it can't return to the centre.
step.d_big.m3: 2.Kc1. The white king starts its walk behind the black king, along the first rank.
step.d_big.m4: 2...Ke2. The black king comes close and takes d1, the square the white king wanted to pass through.
step.d_big.m5: 3.Bg6. A waiting move: the bishop stays on the diagonal, and the black king, which has to move, must leave e2.
step.d_big.m6: 3...Ke3. Now d1 is free for the white king.
step.d_big.m7: 4.Kd1. One more step of the walk. The black king has only f2 and f3.
step.d_big.m8: 4...Kf2. The black king heads for h1, the corner of the bishop's colour. That's where we want it.
step.bigWalk: Continue the white king's walk to f4, always next to the black king. Four moves.
step.bigWalk.hint: One square at a time, along the second and then the third rank, never letting the black king back towards d1.
step.bigWalk.done: 8.Kf4! The white king has completed its walk: it takes g3, g4 and g5 from the inside, and the black king has only h3. After 8...Kh3, the triangle can shrink.
step.t_mid: After 8...Kh3, the black king is trapped in the big triangle and your king has reached f4. How do you make the triangle shrink?
step.t_mid.hint1: There is a smaller light diagonal, closer to h1, that also cuts across the black king's path.
step.t_mid.hint2: Count the squares the black king can reach: does it get to the smaller diagonal before you close it?
step.mid: 9.Bh5 is the jump. Delétang's rule for every phase is a single one: the bishop jumps to the smaller diagonal when the black king can no longer reach the new one. Here the black king, on h3, can't step on any square of the d1–h5 diagonal: g4 belongs to the white king, and the others are far away. After the jump, the triangle runs from e1 to h1 and up to h4. The dangerous point is e1, from where the black king would escape via d2; that's why the knight hurries from e6 to e4, via c5, to close d2, f2 and g3.
step.d_mid: Watch the bishop's jump and the knight's race.
step.d_mid.m1: 9.Bh5. The bishop jumps to the d1–h5 diagonal. The black king has g2, h2 and h4, inside the middle triangle.
step.d_mid.m2: 9...Kg2. The black king runs towards e1, the point of the triangle closest to the exit.
step.d_mid.m3: 10.Nc5. The knight leaves e6, which is no longer needed, and heads for e4.
step.d_mid.m4: 10...Kf2. One more step towards e1 and d2.
step.d_mid.m5: 11.Ne4+. With check, the knight arrives in time and closes d2, f2 and g3. The black king can no longer leave the triangle.
step.d_mid.m6: 11...Kg2. The black king steps out of check and stays near the corner.
step.d_mid.m7: 12.Bg4. The bishop stays on the diagonal and now also takes h3 from the black king. That frees the white king to leave f4.
step.midWalk: After 12...Kf1, the white king makes its second walk, round the outside of the middle triangle, until it stands next to f1. Four moves. It's Seirawan's wall from lesson I, on the h1 side: the wall stays put and only the white king moves.
step.midWalk.hint: Along the third rank and then the second, always next to the black king, never leaving it e1 or d2.
step.midWalk.done: 16.Ke2! The king takes f1 and f2, the knight takes f2 and g3, and the black king has only g1, h1 and h2. After 16...Kg1, the bishop's last jump is all that's left.
step.t_small: After 16...Kg1, the black king moves between g1, g2, h1 and h2. Which bishop move closes the last triangle without losing the bishop?
step.t_small.hint1: The last light diagonal before the corner is the shortest of all, with three squares.
step.t_small.hint2: If the black king attacks the bishop, it can retreat along the same diagonal to a square your king defends.
step.small: 17.Bh3 closes the third triangle, the small one, based on the f1–h3 diagonal. The bishop takes g2 from the black king; the king on e2 takes f1 and f2; the knight on e4 takes f2 and g3. Only h1 and h2 remain. On h3 the bishop can be attacked, but it retreats to f1, on the same diagonal, protected by the king. It's the c7 net from lesson I, seen from the h1 corner: the bishop drops back from h3 to f1 and the knight heads for f3, just as it headed for c6 there. What changes is the mate: here the knight checks and the bishop finishes.
step.smallWalk: Close the last triangle, as in lesson I's c7 net: the bishop closes the diagonal, drops back if attacked, and the knight heads for f3. Three moves.
step.smallWalk.hint: The bishop goes to h3 and, if attacked, drops back along the same diagonal to the square your king defends. Then the knight heads for f3, via g5.
step.smallWalk.done: 19.Ng5! The knight heads for f3, from where it checks on h2 and takes g1. After 19...Kh1, the black king is in the corner, and only the mate is left.
step.mateH1: Deliver mate. Three moves: the king closes in, the knight checks, the bishop finishes.
step.mateH1.hint: First the king goes to f2, to take g1 and g2. Then the knight check pushes the black king back to h1.
step.mateH1.done: 22.Bg2#. The bishop checks on h1, the knight on f3 takes g1 and h2, and the king on f2 protects the bishop. That's the mating pattern in the h1 corner. Mind the order: with the black king on h1, 20.Nf3?? is stalemate; the king goes to f2 first.
step.t_seal: Another position. The bishop on e2 is already on the d1–h5 diagonal, the base of the middle triangle, and the black king is on g3, inside it. But the triangle isn't closed yet. Where does the black king get out, and how do you close that exit?
step.t_seal.hint1: The bishop only watches light squares. Look for the dark squares next to the diagonal that the black king can reach.
step.t_seal.hint2: Both exits are on the fourth rank. One of your pieces can take them both in a single move.
step.seal: The black king gets out via f4, or via h4 and then g5: dark squares. A light-squared bishop never covers them: the dark squares next to the diagonal are the job of the knight and the king. 1.Ng6 takes f4 and h4 at once, without the bishop having to move; then the white king comes to d2 and closes e1 and e3. Until now the net came ready-made; now you build it, and the rule is this: the bishop's diagonal only traps the king when the dark squares next to it are closed too.
step.d_sealWrong: First, see what happens if the bishop goes first, to the big diagonal, with the dark squares still open.
step.d_sealWrong.m1: 1.Bd3? The bishop goes to the b1–h7 diagonal, but gives up f3 and g4, and the dark squares f4 and h4 are still open.
step.d_sealWrong.m2: 1...Kf4! f4 is dark, and no white piece watches it. The black king is already out of the triangle.
step.d_sealWrong.m3: 2.Nf7. The knight arrives too late, to take e5 and g5.
step.d_sealWrong.m4: 2...Ke3. The black king attacks the bishop and enters the centre from the other side.
step.d_sealWrong.m5: 3.Bf5. The bishop escapes the attack, but d4 is still open.
step.d_sealWrong.m6: 3...Kd4. The black king has reached the centre of the board. White still wins, but the work of driving it to the edge starts over. With 1.Ng6, it would never have left the h1 side.
step.sealRight: Now close the exit the right way and bring the king. Two moves.
step.sealRight.hint: The exits are dark: only the knight takes them both at once. Then the white king comes along the second rank.
step.sealRight.done: 2.Kd2! The knight on g6 takes f4 and h4, the bishop closes the diagonal, and the white king takes e1 and e3. The black king has only g1, g2 and g3, near h1.
step.t_route: The black king, on g4, is still close to the centre, and the bishop is at home on f1. 1.Bd3 puts the bishop on the big diagonal, b1–h7, in a single move. Is there something better?
step.t_route.hint1: After 1.Bd3, which light squares can the black king still reach? Look at h5.
step.t_route.hint2: The black king wants to climb up the h-file. Which diagonal cuts that road without giving up a light square?
step.route: 1.Be2+! The bishop enters the d1–h5 diagonal with check. The check takes g4 and h5 from the black king; the knight on e6 takes f4 and g5; the king on e4 takes f3. The black king is left with g3, h3 and h4, inside the middle triangle. The big diagonal looked more natural, but from d3 the bishop gives up h5, and that's the way the black king climbs out. Before choosing the diagonal, look at where the black king wants to go.
step.d_routeWrong: First, watch the bishop go straight to the big diagonal.
step.d_routeWrong.m1: 1.Bd3? The bishop enters the b1–h7 diagonal, but from d3 it doesn't watch h5.
step.d_routeWrong.m2: 1...Kh5! The light square h5 has been left unguarded, and the black king climbs out through it.
step.d_routeWrong.m3: 2.Ke5. The white king comes to take f6, but the black king has already left the h1 side.
step.d_routeWrong.m4: 2...Kh6. The black king is now near h8, the wrong corner for a light-squared bishop.
step.d_routeWrong.m5: 3.Bf5. The bishop takes g4 and g6, and the black king is stuck on the h-file. White still wins, but the king has to be brought all the way back to h1, and every move counts towards the fifty.
step.routeRight: Now the right way: close the middle triangle with tempo and put the bishop in safety. Two moves.
step.routeRight.hint: The first move is a check. Then the bishop stays on the same diagonal, next to your king.
step.routeRight.done: 2.Bf3! The bishop stays on the d1–h5 diagonal, protected by the king on e4, and takes g2 from the black king. The black king is in the middle triangle; as in the second chapter, the knight still has to close d2 and f2.
step.t_loose: Your pieces are scattered: the king and bishop are still at home, and the knight has gone too far, to c8, next to the black king, which attacks it. Save the knight and, if you can, gain time. What's the move?
step.t_loose.hint1: Retreating the knight saves it, but costs time. There is a move that defends the knight and forces the black king to move.
step.t_loose.hint2: Look for a check. Once the black king steps out of the way, who will be looking at c8?
step.loose: 1.Bh3+! The bishop checks along the h3–c8 diagonal, which passes through the black king and ends on the knight. The black king has to leave it, and then the bishop defends c8. Retreating the knight to b6 or a7 also saves it, but the black king keeps hunting, and the white king is still far away. In lesson II the rule was to protect before advancing, and in one of its exercises 2.Bc4+ already defended the knight with check; here the piece is already attacked, and the check through the king saves it and gains a tempo. Then the white king comes close to the pieces: a piece far from its king is a target.
step.d_loose: Watch the knight escape with tempo and the white king arrive.
step.d_loose.m1: 1.Bh3+! Check and defence at once. The black king has to leave the diagonal.
step.d_loose.m2: 1...Kc6. The black king steps out of check, but c8 is now defended by the bishop.
step.d_loose.m3: 2.Ne7+. The knight leaves the edge with check, giving the black king no time.
step.d_loose.m4: 2...Kc5. The black king steps out of check and heads for the centre.
step.d_loose.m5: 3.Ng6. The knight goes to a square the black king can't reach any time soon.
step.d_loose.m6: 3...Kb4. The black king no longer has any white piece within reach.
step.d_loose.m7: 4.Kd2. Now the white king comes and takes c3 from the black king. The knight and bishop are out of its reach, and the white king arrives to bring the three pieces together.
step.loose2: Another position: the black king, on g6, attacks the knight on h5. Save the knight with tempo and bring the king. Two moves.
step.loose2.hint: Look for the check that passes through the black king and reaches the knight. Then the white king approaches through the centre.
step.loose2.done: 1.Be8+! The black king leaves g6, and the bishop defends h5 along the e8–h5 diagonal. After 1...Kf5, 2.Kd4 brings the king close to the pieces and takes e4 and e5 from the black king.
step.t_rhine: Now the traps. Near the right corner, the check 1.Nb6+ looks natural. Before checking, look at the black king's squares and the bishop's safety. What's the move?
step.t_rhine.hint1: Imagine the check and find the square the black king runs to. What does it attack from there?
step.t_rhine.hint2: If the bishop is attacked next to the black king, where can it go without leaving the black king with no moves?
step.rhine: This is a trap the American master Frederick Rhine showed in a chess magazine in 2000. After 1.Nb6+??, the black king goes to d8 and attacks the bishop on e8, which nothing defends. Every move that saves the bishop leaves the black king with no move and not in check: stalemate. The right move is a king move, 1.Ke7, which protects the bishop and takes d7 and d8 from the black king. Near the corner, before every check, count the squares the black king has left.
step.d_rhine: Watch the reply after 1.Nb6+??, the hasty check. Now it's the black king's turn, and it saves the draw.
step.d_rhine.m1: 1...Kd8! The black king attacks the bishop, and no white piece defends e8.
step.d_rhine.m2: 2.Bf7. The bishop is safe, but the black king has no move and is not in check. Stalemate: a draw.
step.rhineRight: Now the right move, without a check.
step.rhineRight.hint: Protect the bishop before any check, or take it out of the black king's reach.
step.rhineRight.done: That wins. 1.Ke7 protects the bishop and takes d7 and d8 from the black king, which is left with b7, b8 and c7. 1.Na5 also wins, and the bishop moves to a4, b5 or c6 take the bishop out of the black king's reach before the check.
step.t_kempinski: Robert Kempinski versus Vladimir Epishin, in the Bundesliga, the German club league, January 2001. Today you play Black, like Epishin: his bishop is dark-squared, the right corners are a1 and h8, and the white king has hidden on the a8 side, the wrong corner. Kempinski has just played 156.Ka6. Look at the squares the white king uses to get back to the corner. How do you drive it down the a-file without letting it return?
step.t_kempinski.hint1: Count the white king's squares: b5, b6 and b7 belong to your king, and a7 to the bishop. Only a5 is left.
step.t_kempinski.hint2: A waiting move won't do: the white king would just stay on a6. Find a move that forces it to a5 right now, without giving up a7.
step.kempinski: How they got here: on move 126 Epishin captured White's last piece, 126...Nxd3, and was left with king, bishop and knight against the bare king. Kempinski ran with his king to a8 and, from 140.Ka8 on, kept circling the corner, between a8, a7, b8 and a6. In lesson I, Karttunen drove the black king along the edge with the W; here the white king sticks to the corner, and the danger is stalemate. The rule for getting it out of the wrong corner: take its squares one at a time and always leave it an exit, away from the corner. After 150.Ka5, the annotators give 150...Nd5!, which takes b4 and prepares a check if the white king goes back to a6. Epishin played 150...Kc5?, the white king went back to the corner, and the same position only came back after 155.Ka5. This time he found 155...Nd5!, and Kempinski answered 156.Ka6. Now 156...Nb4+! takes a6 from the white king and leaves it only a5, further down.
step.d_kempinski: What Epishin played in the game.
step.d_kempinski.m1: 156...Bc7? The bishop leaves b8 and gives up a7, the square through which the white king returns to the corner.
step.d_kempinski.m2: 157.Ka7. The white king climbs back up.
step.d_kempinski.m3: 157...Bb6+. The check takes a7 from the white king, but it still has a6, a8 and b8.
step.d_kempinski.m4: 158.Kb8. The white king sticks to the corner again.
step.kempinskiNc7: After 158.Kb8, the white king is glued to the corner again. What's the move?
step.kempinskiNc7.hint: The white king has only a8 and c8. Take the corner square away from it and leave the other as an exit, away from the corner.
step.kempinskiNc7.done: 158...Nc7! The knight covers a8, and the white king has to leave via c8, away from the corner. It was the fastest road. In the game Epishin played 158...Bc5?, and with it the mate no longer fitted within the fifty moves: the white king went back to a8, after 176...Nb6 Kempinski could already claim a draw, and with 179...Nc8 the white king was stalemated. A draw.
step.recap: Keep three rules. One: the bishop closes the diagonal, and the dark squares next to it belong to the knight and the king; the diagonal alone doesn't trap anything. Two: the bishop only jumps to the smaller diagonal when the black king can no longer reach it, and it picks the diagonal by looking at where the black king wants to go. Three: before every check, count the black king's squares and see what it attacks; and in the wrong corner, always leave it an exit.
step.finish: Your turn, in the practical challenge: the whole mate, from the start. Drive the black king to the edge as in lesson II, use the W if it runs to the wrong corner, and close the triangles to finish.
ex.e04: The knight on d3 and the king on g6 are already in place. Which bishop move closes the first triangle? Find the winning move.
ex.e04.hint: The first triangle's diagonal runs from a2 to g8. The bishop must stand on it, on a safe square.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Bb3 puts the bishop on the a2–g8 diagonal, and the black king is locked in the a2–a8–g8 triangle. Any safe square on the diagonal will do: a2, c4, f7 or g8 work the same. The knight on d3 covers b4 and c5; the king on g6 covers f6, f7 and g7.
ex.e12: The bishop sits in the a8 corner and the black king is close by. A knight check is right there. What is the move? Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: Before you check, find the square the black king runs to and see what it attacks from there. Sometimes the right move is a king move.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kc6 wins: the white king takes b7, c7 and d7, and the black king is left with b8 and d8. 1.Nd6+ would be the lesson's trap in new clothes: 1...Kb8! attacks the bishop, every bishop move is stalemate, and any other move lets the black king capture the bishop. Draw. Near the corner, count the black king's squares before every check.
ex.e16: The black king is already on the h1 side. To close the big triangle, the bishop has to reach the b1–h7 diagonal and the knight has to plug the dark squares next to it. Which piece goes first? Two moves. Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: Picture the bishop on g6 right now and find the black king's answer. Through which dark square does he head back to the centre?
ex.e16.solution: 1.Ne6! first: the knight takes f4 and g5, and the black king has no way back to the centre. After 1...Kg4, 2.Bg6! closes the b1–h7 diagonal, and the black king is left with h4, h3, g3 and f3, inside the big triangle. With 1.Bg6? straight away, 1...Kf4! and the black king threatens to slip out through e5; the net costs several extra moves. The order matters: first the dark squares, then the diagonal.
ex.e13: Kempinski versus Epishin, Bundesliga 2001: today the bishop and knight are yours, with Black. The white king is hiding on a8, the wrong corner for a dark-squared bishop. Get it out of there without stalemating it. Two moves. Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: The white king only has a7, b7 and b8 around it, and you already cover two of them. Don't take the last one: bring the knight to a square where it takes a8.
ex.e13.solution: 140...Nc4! and, after 141.Ka7, the only move, 141...Nb6! The knight takes a8 and the white king has to step out to a6, away from the wrong corner. After 142.Ka6, 142...Bb8! takes a7, and the white king has to go on to a5, further and further from the corner. 140...Kb6, 140...Nb5 and 140...Nc8 are stalemate on the spot, and 140...Bb8 lets the king capture the bishop. In the game Epishin played 140...Bd8?, let the white king back into the wrong corner more than once and, when his opponent could already claim a draw under the fifty-move rule, ended up stalemating the white king.
ex.e14: The central position of the old treatises, which Daniel Delétang solved with his triangles in his 1923 article: black king on f4, your three pieces side by side. Bring the bishop to the b1–h7 diagonal without giving the black king a single spare square. Three moves. Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: 1.Bd3 is already on the diagonal, but it lets go of f5 and g4. Find a route on which the bishop watches those two squares all the way.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Be6! is the only move on the shortest path: the bishop takes f5 and g4, the knight covers g3 and g5, the king covers e3 and e5, and the black king only has f3. After 1...Kf3, 2.Bf5 (2.Ng5+ and 2.Nd6 also do); after 2...Kf4, 3.Bg6 (or 3.Nd6). The bishop has reached the b1–h7 diagonal, the base of the big triangle, and the black king is on the h1 side, the right corner. This is how Delétang begins the solution he believed could not be shortened. 1.Bd3, straight to the diagonal, lets the black king out through f5 or g4.
ex.e15: The black king is in the centre, and your pieces are far from your king and from each other. He is going to attack them. Three moves to save everything without losing time. Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: Find the square from which the black king would attack the bishop and the knight at once, and take it away. After that, every move has to defend the attacked piece, ideally gaining time.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kd4! takes e3 and e4 from the black king. Bishop moves now lose a piece: 1.Bd3? Ke3 attacks both, 1.Be4? and 1.Bf5? are within the king's reach, and so is 1.Ng4? After 1...Kf3 the knight is attacked and goes to a safe square: 2.Nh1 (or 2.Ne4, 2.Nd1, 2.Nd3). If 2...Kg2, attacking the knight on h1, only 3.Be4+ saves it: the check drives the black king off g2, and the bishop on e4 now defends h1 along the long diagonal. Any other move loses the knight, and king and bishop alone cannot mate.
key.net1: The first triangle, the big one: bishop, knight and king together close off a piece of the corner, and the black king can't get out.
key.net2: The second triangle, smaller: the white pieces close in and the black king's space shrinks.
key.net3: The third triangle, the smallest of all: the black king has only three squares in the corner, and mate is near.
key.deletangStart: The start of the triangle method: the bishop builds a barrier along a diagonal, and the black king can no longer cross it.
key.rhineTrap: A stalemate trap: a hasty knight check leaves the bishop stuck next to the black king. Any bishop move stalemates, and anything else loses the bishop.
key.practiceStart: The starting point of the full mate: White's pieces on their home squares and the black king on the far side of the board.
key.kempinski: Kempinski versus Epishin, German Bundesliga, 2001: Black has bishop and knight, and the white king hides near a8, the corner where there is no mate. Epishin didn't get it out of there in time, and the game ended in a draw, with the white king stalemated.
history: This lesson puts it all together: from the start, with the pieces far apart, to mate in the right corner. The method is Daniel Delétang's triangles, from an article he wrote in Buenos Aires and published in the magazine La Stratégie in 1923: the bishop closes a diagonal, the other pieces block the squares next to it, and the opposing king is trapped in three ever smaller triangles. It isn't the shortest road, but it's easy to remember and fits within the fifty-move limit. It's an ending that looks like a sure win and isn't. In 2001, in the German Bundesliga, grandmaster Vladimir Epishin had bishop and knight against Robert Kempinski's bare king, didn't find the mate, let the fifty moves pass and ended up stalemating his opponent's king: a draw.
practice: Enough script. The black king is already near h1, the right corner. Close the triangles or play the W, as you prefer, and deliver the mate. Then the same ending in the speedrun, against the clock.
